blocks.text: …the people who own the plant where we got sick."
I looked at the other five bags. Then I started unzipping them. All five people inside were breathing, barely. They were unconscious and very cold.
I turned the refrigeration off, wrapped them in every blanket in my cab, and called 911 again. This time I didn't hang up when my employer called. I let it ring.
Paramedics arrived twelve minutes later. All six were taken to the hospital with hypothermia. All six survived.

The young man who grabbed my arm was named Jorge. He was nineteen. He and the others worked the night shift at a chemical plant outside Houston. A week earlier, a valve failed and released a toxic cloud inside the building. Six workers were exposed and fell seriously ill.
Instead of calling an ambulance, the plant's managers took them to a private clinic owned by the company.

The plant had already been fined twice for safety violations. Another accident would have shut it down. So the managers made a terrible plan: list the six workers as having died in a "vehicle accident," sedate them for transport, and move them to San Antonio, where a contractor would put them on a bus to the border. All six were undocumented. The managers assumed no one would ask questions.
The bags and stretchers came from the clinic. The cold was meant to keep them sedated. Jorge had woken up early.

OSHA and federal prosecutors opened an investigation the next day. The plant's general manager, two supervisors, and the clinic's doctor were charged with assault, false imprisonment, and conspiracy. The plant was shut down.
All six workers received special visas as crime victims and are pursuing a lawsuit against the company. Jorge calls me every few months. He's training to be an electrician.
I never got the $1,500. I don't want it.
If you suspect human trafficking or labor exploitation, call the National Human Trafficking Hotline at 1-888-373-7888.
